title: The Evolution of the Gem
author: Dr Dario Emanuele
summary: Dario Emanuele follows up his earlier post introducing a Gemini Gem for lesson planning with a worked example of what the improved tool can now do. Planning a Year 9 lesson on changing the subject of a formula, he imposed a strict constraint to manage intrinsic load, giving the Gem one exit-ticket question as the standard students had to master. He reports that the Gem produced a complete atomisation that fit his slide template, scripted explanatory language (distinguishing the 'loose' term from the 'attached' term), and generated a bespoke practice question set matched to the model's mechanics. Borrowing an idea from Dylan Wiliam, he then had the Gem write LaTeX code that compiles in Overleaf into a textbook-quality worksheet with graduated challenge. The piece argues that a teacher-built AI assistant can take over the most time-consuming parts of lesson preparation, and closes by naming the remaining gap, automatic slide generation, and asking readers for tools.
points: Emanuele frames the Gem's value through a cognitive-load constraint: one tightly specified exit-ticket question defined the lesson rather than a generic 'rearranging' topic.

The Gem's output went beyond planning to scripting teacher language, such as separating the 'loose' +3b term from the 'attached' coefficient of x, which he treats as misconception-preventing explicit instruction.
Generating a bespoke question bank matched to the model replaced his usual trawl through several websites for suitable practice items.
The LaTeX-via-Overleaf workflow, borrowed from Dylan Wiliam, turns the Gem into a worksheet generator without snipping or manual formatting.
Slides remain the unsolved step: NotebookLM could not auto-generate decks and alternatives were paid or poor, so he crowdsources a solution.
quotes: But here is the thing about AI: it moves fast. Since that post, the arrival of Gemini 3.0 combined with the continuous “feeding” of my research documents into the system has improved the Gem’s performance. The quality of the atomisation and the structural logic for lesson slides has jumped to a new level.

I needed to plan a lesson for my Year 9 class on changing the subject of a formula. If you are a maths teacher, you definitely know this is a vast topic. The sheer variety of question types can easily lead to cognitive overload, which is exactly why we revisit it in Year 10 and 11, too.
I wanted to apply a strict constraint to manage the intrinsic load. I didn’t want a generic “rearranging” lesson.

It scripted the explanation: It suggested specific language to scaffold the learning, such as distinguishing between the “loose” term (the +3b that must be moved first) and the “attached” term (the coefficient of x to be dealt with last). This is exactly the kind of explicit instruction that clears up misconceptions before they happen.

It generated the perfect question set: Usually, I have to trawl through three or four websites to find a bank of questions that matches exactly the mechanics of my model. The Gem generated a bespoke list of practice questions based precisely on the y=9ax+3b structure.
The takeaway: The Gem I shared with you isn’t just a lesson planner. It is a worksheet generator. Don’t be intimidated by the word “LaTeX”, it is intuitive.

As full-time teachers, we need to save every second we can. Right now, I am still manually building the Google Slides based on the text the Gem gives me. I tried NotebookLM, hoping it could auto-generate a deck, but that feature isn’t currently available (and I’m too impatient to wait!).
